hints: Look at the ring of oval structures in Fig. 1.1 - each one is a vascular bundle containing both xylem and phloem, so think about which side faces the centre of the stem.
walkthrough:
Recall Stem Bundle Layout**
Think of the stem in transverse section with the pith in the middle and the cortex outside. Each vascular bundle has phloem on the outside and xylem on the inside.

Place Your Label**
Draw a label line to the inner half of any one of the eight bundles in Fig. 1.1 and write X. That inner region is xylem vessels and associated xylem tissue.
Final answer: Label line with X to xylem tissue on the inner side of a vascular bundle (towards the centre / pith of the stem).

hints: Start from what holds one water molecule to the next water molecule, and what happens at the leaf when water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls.
Think about what the word cohesion means for pulling - if the top molecule is pulled up and out, what must happen to the molecules hydrogen-bonded to it below?
Link this pulling effect to a continuous column that can move upward against gravity in a narrow xylem vessel.
walkthrough:
Cohesion From Hydrogen Bonds**
Water is polar, so hydrogen bonds form between water molecules. This attraction between identical molecules is called cohesion, so neighbouring water molecules stick strongly to each other.

Pull Transmitted Down The Column**
When water evaporates from leaves, water is removed from the top of the xylem. Because of cohesion, the departing molecules drag the molecules below them upward. This is transpiration pull.

Continuous Column Up The Stem**
The result is an unbroken, continuous column of water in the xylem vessels that can be pulled upward to the leaves, even against the pull of gravity.

Final answer: Hydrogen bonds cause cohesion between water molecules; water lost at the top pulls water below upward, creating transpiration pull and maintaining a continuous column of water up the xylem against gravity.

hints: Follow the arrows in Fig. 1.2 - water goes from cell A into B and then into C without leaving the living cytoplasm, so which direct cytoplasm-to-cytoplasm connections allow this?
Recall the name for movement through connected cytoplasm and vacuoles, and think about what must be true about water potential in B compared to A for net flow A to B.
Remember that entering the large central vacuole means crossing a specific membrane by osmosis - what is that membrane called?
walkthrough:
Describe The Route - Symplast**
The arrows show water passing directly from cytoplasm to cytoplasm between adjacent cells. That happens through plasmodesmata, the narrow cytoplasmic strands linking plant cells. This is the symplastic / cytoplasmic pathway, including movement through vacuoles via the vacuolar pathway.

Explain The Direction - Water Potential**
Net movement is always down a water potential gradient, from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential. So cell B has lower water potential than A, and cell C has lower water potential than B.

Crossing Into Vacuoles By Osmosis**
To move into and out of the large central vacuole shown in Fig. 1.2, water crosses the tonoplast membrane by osmosis, continuing the symplastic flow toward the lower water potential.

Final answer: Water moves A to B to C via plasmodesmata through the symplast / cytoplasm including the vacuolar pathway; water moves down a water potential gradient from higher to lower water potential, entering / leaving vacuoles by osmosis across the tonoplast.

hints: Ask yourself what surrounds every plant cell on the outside and what fills most of the volume inside that an animal cell never has.
Think about the membrane around that large fluid-filled space and where the nucleus gets pushed as a result.
Recall the tiny cytoplasmic links between adjacent plant cells that you used in (c)(i) and that are just visible with good light microscopy.
walkthrough:
Wall And Vacuole - The Obvious Clues**
Under high power you can see a distinct cell wall outside the cell surface membrane, which animals lack. Inside, a large permanent vacuole occupies most of the cell volume, bounded by the tonoplast.

Pushed-Aside Nucleus**
Because the vacuole is so large, the cytoplasm forms only a thin layer and the nucleus is pushed to the edge or periphery of the cell, unlike the central nucleus typical of many animal cells.

Connections Between Cells**
You can also see plasmodesmata, the cytoplasmic strands crossing the walls between adjacent cells. Together these features confirm a plant parenchyma cell, not an animal cell.
Final answer: Cell wall; large permanent vacuole (with tonoplast); nucleus at periphery / edge of cell; plasmodesmata between adjacent cells.
